title: Size Ladder: Circular Wardrobes for GLP-1 Users
angle: Pairing 1: GLP-1/consumer health x Textile circular economy
one_liner: A subscription that ships the next clothing size on the GLP-1 titration schedule, takes back the last, stores a 'restart' wardrobe, and routes the excess into resale and recycling, sold through telehealth partners as a retention perk.
customer: Cash-pay GLP-1 patients ($59-129 a month), telehealth and clinic operators paying a per-member fee for retention, and plus-size apparel brands and textile-EPR schemes that need diverted volume.
problem: Users move through three to five sizes in 12-18 months, and only about a third are still on therapy at one year while roughly 60% of ex-users plan to restart and stoppers regain about two thirds within a year. So closets fill with clothes that fit neither the current body nor the likely future one. The US textile recycling rate is 14.7% and California alone landfills 1.2M tons a year. Telehealth players have converged on the same $149-$349 price, so they need non-price loyalty features.
solution: At each dose step or every 10 lb, ship the next size from a pooled inventory of pre-owned and new pieces, take back the previous size, and offer take-in tailoring as an alternative. A 'restart wardrobe' bank holds the prior size for 12 months for a small fee. With consent, the telehealth partner shares titration stage so the platform can forecast sizes; in return the clinician sees a behavioral signal when size changes stall or reverse.
why_now: Cash-pay pills at $149 have widened the user base (22% of households have a user) and moved buying away from insurers to consumers who are already spending more on skincare and fragrance. California's textile EPR (SB 707) is moving toward fee-setting, creating a funded outlet for take-back volume. Compounding's exit has pushed users onto branded cash-pay channels that want stickiness.
revenue_model: Consumer subscription, partner PMPM fees ($3-6) from telehealth for retention, brand sponsorship from apparel companies, and resale margin plus EPR diversion credits on the outflow.
non_obvious_insight: Titration is a clock. Because dose steps predict weight-loss milestones, the apparel demand curve is forecastable in a way no fashion category ever is, and the closet is the earliest behavioral read-out of regain.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 patients from GLP-1 patient communities and one partner clinic. Source pre-owned plus-size inventory cheaply from thrift and textile sorters. Line up a tailor network. Run a 3-month pilot at $79 a month, tracking return rates, size churn and how well titration stage predicts the next size.

title: Small-Claims Autopilot for Unpaid Invoices
one_liner: Take a solo operator from unpaid invoice to demand letter, filing, service, hearing prep and enforcement in a self-help flow.
customer: Freelancers, contractors and small B2B suppliers with $1k-20k unpaid invoices and no lawyer.
problem: Chasing fails, lawyers cost more than the claim, and small-claims procedure (forms, service, evidence, hearing, enforcement) is confusing, so most owners write off the debt. Cash is tight: nonemployers are less likely to be profitable and lean on personal funds.
solution: Connect invoices, email and texts. The system builds an evidence timeline, verifies the debtor entity and registered agent through state records, drafts a statutory-interest demand letter, files via e-filing where supported, schedules service, and prepares a hearing script and enforcement steps (garnishment and lien templates). It runs as a self-help tool, with a partner attorney for contested cases.
why_now: LLMs read messy invoice and message threads, e-filing is expanding in many courts, and nonemployer cash flow is under stress.
revenue_model: $79 flat per claim plus 10-15% of amounts collected, or a subscription for repeat filers.
non_obvious_insight: The demand letter itself resolves a large share of cases, and enforcement of the judgment is where the value sits, so the product should cover the full path. The regulatory edge is self-help positioning and attorney partners (the FTC's DoNotPay order shows the limits; prior knowledge).
first_30_days: Pick two states with online filing and $10k-plus limits. Run 30 claims for freelancers and trades sourced from community groups, and publish recovery rates and time to payment.

title: Recurring-Gift Migration Concierge for Churches
one_liner: A fixed-fee service that moves a church's recurring donors off an expensive or hostile giving platform without losing them.
customer: Churches of 100-2,000 weekly attendees paying Pushpay, Subsplash, Tithe.ly or Ministry Brands. The buyer is the pastor, executive pastor or volunteer treasurer.
problem: Recurring gifts are the hostage. Donors' saved cards and bank accounts live inside the incumbent platform, and cancelling is punished. A Pushpay reviewer says the church is 'locked into paying $350/mo for nothing since we've migrated over to the new giving platform.' A Subsplash reviewer reports 'nearly $500 just to stop their services.' Another Subsplash reviewer, on Feb 1, 2026, says they were billed and overdrawn after trying to cancel before the 1/31 renewal. A Tithe.ly app reviewer, on Jul 2, 2026, says the company keeps debiting the account after it was closed. Another Tithe.ly reviewer says there is no way to refund a transaction sent to the wrong place.
solution: Six steps. (1) A free fee audit: upload 3 processor statements and get the effective rate, hidden monthly minimums and the card-versus-ACH mix. (2) Run the PCI-compliant card-on-file transfer to a lower-cost processor. Stripe documents this import path, which needs the old processor to release the data and can take days to weeks. (3) Run a text and email campaign that gets each donor to re-enroll in one tap when their data cannot transfer. (4) Send the cancellation notices in writing at the right time and get confirmation of no further debits. (5) Run a 90-day watch for double billing and stray debits. (6) Add ongoing recovery of failed recurring gifts.
why_now: Reviews dated 2025-2026 show AI-only support and billing disputes across the major church giving vendors. Tithe.ly reviewers cite 'an AI bot only' and a chatbot that 'freezes up'. Stripe has made bulk card-data imports a documented process, so the technical barrier is lower than it was. Year-end giving season is the peak, so churches decide in Q4 and switch in January to avoid splitting the annual giving statement year.
revenue_model: A fixed migration fee of $1,500-$4,000 per church, or 25% of the first year's verified fee savings. A $49/month giving-health add-on that retries failed recurring gifts and flags stray debits. Possible processor partner revenue, disclosed to the church.
non_obvious_insight: Churches are not stuck because the software is good. They are stuck because moving donors looks impossible, and vendors profit from that fear. The technical part is solved, since Stripe documents importing cards and ACH from a prior processor at https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/data-migrations/pan-import. What is missing is a human to run donor communications and paperwork. Evidence: Pushpay ($350/month lock-in after migrating, sales promises that differ from the contract) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/pushpay.com. Subsplash (about $500 exit penalty, overdraft after cancellation, $800 stuck 'pending') at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/subsplash.com. Tithe.ly (debits after closure, no refund path for errors) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=694740700/sortby=mostrecent/xml and https://www.trustpilot.com/review/tithe.ly. Church administrators also trade advice in denominational networks and Facebook groups, so a good migration spreads by word of mouth cheaply.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the fee-audit calculator as a spreadsheet plus a landing page, and pull the public Pushpay, Subsplash and Tithe.ly reviewers. Days 10-20: offer 20 churches the free audit through church-admin Facebook groups and denominational finance offices. Days 20-30: sign 2-3 pilot churches for a January migration and pre-sell in Q4. Confirm with a payments attorney that the transfer flow keeps the service out of PCI scope, meaning it never touches card numbers.

title: Diabetes Desk: Remote Glucose-Curve Review for Clinics
one_liner: CGMs and once-daily insulins made diabetic pets manageable at home, but nobody owns the workflow; sell clinics an outsourced desk that reads curves and proposes titrations for the DVM to approve.
customer: General-practice clinics with a dozen or more insulin-dependent dogs and cats. Secondary: pet insurers with diabetic cohorts.
problem: AAHA's 2026 guidelines split canine and feline diabetes for the first time and emphasize CGMs and once-daily insulins (degludec, glargine U-300). Owner burden is high and remote-monitoring services are thin. Clinics get a stream of curves they have neither the time nor a billing model to review, so pets stay poorly regulated. Tight control gives diabetic cats a real chance of remission, and avoids expensive ketoacidosis emergencies.
solution: Owners link a CGM to a clinic-branded portal. A desk of RVTs plus a consulting internist reviews curves weekly, flags hypoglycemia risk, and drafts dose-change suggestions for the clinic's own vet to approve within their VCPR. Includes SMS coaching on feeding and injection technique and refill/supply coordination. The clinic bills the owner a monthly program fee and pays us a wholesale share.
why_now: 2026 AAHA guidelines make CGM standard-of-care thinking. Long-acting insulins reduce injection burden. Ambient AI makes the record-keeping cheap, and remote-care rules are loosening piecemeal.
revenue_model: Clinic charges owners $59-99 per month; we take about $30-45 per patient per month. Later: outcome-based contracts with insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The clinical tech (CGMs, insulins, guidelines) arrived before the operating model. Human remote-monitoring took years to get billing codes; in vet medicine the owner pays directly and the value (fewer ER visits) is visible immediately, so a desk business can start without any payer.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 clinics and about 20 diabetic patients. Run a manual desk with one contract RVT and a part-time internist consult. Use CGM sharing links or screenshots to start. Track time-in-range and ER visits, and price the pilot at $79 per month.

title: Solar Closing Desk for Listing Agents
one_liner: A per-listing service that clears solar leases, PPAs, loans and UCC-1 fixture filings before the house hits the MLS, so escrow does not blow up in week three.
customer: Listing agents, brokerages and title/escrow firms in solar-dense counties (CA, AZ, FL, TX, NJ, MA, CO, NV, HI). The seller pays $395-795 per listing at closing from proceeds, or a brokerage pays a flat subscription.
problem: Solar lease and PPA transfers need provider consent, which can add 2-6 weeks to escrow and sometimes fails. Solar UCC-1 fixture filings show up on the title prelim and block closings, refinances and HELOCs. Agents usually discover this on day 20 of escrow, when the buyer's credit check fails or the provider's transfer queue stalls. One industry cite claims about half of agents have had solar complicate a deal. The 2015-2020 lease vintages are now entering resale years, and TPO is the only route to a federal credit since 2026, so volume rises for a decade.
solution: Start the clock at listing, not at contract. Within 48 hours, identify who owns the system using permit data, UCC search, the title prelim and a monitoring-account check. Order the provider's payoff and transfer packet. Soft-pre-qualify likely buyers in the provider's portal. Produce a one-page Solar Fact Sheet for the MLS with verified production history, remaining term, escalator and buyout cost. Then run the chosen path: payoff and UCC-3 termination, transfer with consent, or subordination to the new mortgage. Provide escrow instructions and agent scripts, and offer buyout financing through a partner.
why_now: TPO has become the dominant way to buy solar after 25D ended. First-wave lease systems are hitting the resale market, provider servicing is in flux after the Sunnova and SunPower failures (successor servicer SunStrong), and title companies are seeing more fixture-filing holds. Home sales are slow, so agents cannot afford failed escrows.
revenue_model: Flat per-listing fee paid at closing. Referral fee from lease-buyout lenders (about 1% of buyout). White-label subscription for title and escrow companies. Later, sell aggregated solar-adjustment data to appraisers and mortgage investors.
non_obvious_insight: Every provider's transfer team is a queue with known choke points: the buyer's credit pull, the time-limited buyer acceptance window, and UCC-3 termination filing lag. An installer sees this because neighbors' failed sales kill sales for the next solar rep. The fix is operational, not legal. Agents cannot price a lease because they cannot read production guarantees or escalators, so a plain fact sheet makes the solar a selling point instead of a discount.
first_30_days: Interview 15 listing agents in one solar-heavy county. Offer 5 active solar listings handled free in exchange for testimonials. Hire a part-time escrow officer or paralegal. Publish a Solar Home Sale Checklist for agents to get inbound leads. Sign a pilot with two local title companies. Use manual processes and one shared spreadsheet, with no software build until 50 listings.

title: Deposit Gate That Kills Korean Bulk-Order Scams
one_liner: A KakaoTalk-native verify-and-deposit link that small Korean restaurants, bakeries and caterers send to any big or suspicious order, since scammers never pay a deposit and real customers do.
customer: Korean self-employed food, bakery, flower and catering owners who take phone or chat bulk orders. They pay ₩9,900/month plus a 1.5-2.5% take rate on deposits. Restaurant and bakery associations, POS vendors and card acquirers are distribution partners.
problem: The 'no-show scam' impersonates a government office, military unit, broadcaster or political party and places a large legitimate-looking order. The scammer then asks the owner to buy unrelated goods from a designated supplier, promising to pay for everything together. The owner pays the fake supplier and loses the money. It is 100% preventable by process, yet owners are alone on the phone and busy.
solution: The owner taps a Kakao chatbot or shortcut during the call. The caller receives a verify-and-deposit link: PASS phone identity, a claimed-organization check against official directories with call-back numbers, and a 10-30% deposit via KakaoPay or Toss. A tripwire flags any request to buy from a third-party supplier, which is the hallmark of stage two of the scheme. Scams die at the deposit step. Legitimate bulk buyers pay a small deposit, which also cuts ordinary no-shows.
why_now: H1 2025 losses were roughly 90% of the whole of 2024, with per-case damage up more than 50% year on year. Scammers keep widening the impersonations to entertainment agencies, broadcasters and political parties. Authorities' advice is already 'ask for a deposit', but nothing operationalizes it for a shop owner. KakaoPay and Toss make micro-deposit links trivial.
revenue_model: ₩9,900/month per shop, plus 1.5-2.5% of each deposit processed. B2B2C licensing to POS and reservation vendors, and fraud-loss underwriting data for card and insurance partners.
non_obvious_insight: The theft is not the food order, it is the redirected procurement in stage two, so a single rule ('never buy from a supplier the customer names') is nearly precision-perfect and a deposit is a perfect filter. Police-reported H1 2025 damage was ₩115.5 billion (1,155억 won) across 3,936 cases, about ₩29M per case (https://www.straightnews.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=311867 and https://www.ccmessage.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=121353). The two-stage method and the government's own advice to require deposits and reject out-of-scope purchases are described at https://www.viva100.com/article/20250623501489. The same article cites a Hyundai Research Institute estimate that ordinary no-shows cost hospitality ₩4.5 trillion a year, so the scam-defense wedge extends into a much larger deposit-booking market.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: Build a Kakao Channel bot that sends a hosted page with PASS auth, a deposit request via a payment gateway such as Toss Payments, and a scam-pattern checklist. Days 8-20: Offer free pilots to 50 shops via bakery, catering and restaurant owner Kakao open-chat groups and the local Food Service Association branch, with a scam-script sticker for the phone. Days 21-30: Convert the pilots that actually used it, publish a first 'blocked scam' tally, and approach one POS vendor and one card-acquirer with a co-branded offer.

title: Notice Red-Team and Pleading Triage for Landlords
one_liner: An adversarial checker that tries to break every eviction notice before it is served, then triages incoming AI-drafted pleadings and prices cash-for-keys exits.
customer: Mid-size operators (500-10,000 units) and the landlord-tenant law firms that serve them on flat-fee matters.
problem: Federal pro se filings topped 41,000 in 2025 against a 23,000 average for 2005-2022, and one tenant filed 22 pleadings in a weekend. Operators pay outside counsel to triage each one while units sit idle, and some conclude cash-for-keys is cheaper than winning. Tenants' AI can find a defective notice in minutes, so procedural errors are now fatal.
solution: An adversarial reviewer checks each notice (cure periods, statutory language, service method, ledger accuracy including banned fees) against jurisdiction rules before service. Inbound pleadings are classified, deadlines docketed, and a 48-hour decision brief compares cost-to-contest with a benchmarked cash-for-keys offer that respects relocation rules. An evidence pack (ledger, communications, inspection logs) is auto-assembled. Licensed attorneys supervise, to avoid unauthorized-practice risk.
why_now: Generative tools have made pro se filings cheap and voluminous, and operators are shrinking staff and leaning on AI leasing, so their record-keeping is thin. Municipal fee bans add new ways a ledger can be wrong.
revenue_model: $3-6 per unit per year platform fee plus $75-250 per triaged matter; law-firm seats at $300-600 per month.
non_obvious_insight: The real cost is not the pleading but the vacant unit while it sits in dispute, so the winning metric is decision speed inside 48 hours. Both sides are now AI-armed, and the defensible edge is an adversarial 'red team' that finds your process defects before the tenant does.
first_30_days: Partner with two landlord-tenant firms in a high-volume market. Build a notice checker for two jurisdictions and run it free on 200 historical notices to show catch-rates. Convert firms to a $500 per month seat and operators to a per-matter fee.

title: FTC Review-Rule Audits for Franchisors
one_liner: Fixed-fee audits that find review gating, incentivised reviews and insider reviews across a franchisor's or dealer group's locations, and in the reputation vendors doing it for them.
customer: General counsel and marketing VPs at franchisors and multi-location operators (auto dealer groups, dental support organisations, home-services and fitness franchises), with reputation-management agencies as channel partners.
problem: The FTC Consumer Review Rule bans review gating, sentiment-conditional incentives, suppression and undisclosed insider reviews, with civil penalties of up to $53,088 per violation. The FTC sent 10 warning letters in Dec 2025 and obtained a $4M order (partly suspended) in July 2026. Local operators often use review-request software that quietly routes unhappy customers away from public sites, and franchisors are exposed to franchisee behaviour.
solution: A 'Rule Ready' audit. Scan Google, Yelp, Facebook and vertical sites across all locations for suspicious bursts, employee reviews and incentive language. Mystery-shop vendors' review-request flows (does a 2-star responder get diverted from Google?). Deliver a risk-ranked location report and remediation playbook, then quarterly monitoring and a vendor certification for compliant review-request software.
why_now: Warning letters (Dec 2025), the first orders (July 2026) and law-firm commentary in mid-2026 show an enforcement pattern taking shape, and Italy's Mar 2026 Trustpilot fine shows the referee itself can be penalised.
revenue_model: $5-25k per audit scaled by location count, $2-8k per month monitoring, and certification fees from review-software vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Liability sits with the buyer of reputation software, not the vendor, and those vendors' flows were designed when gating was legal. The money follows the risk to the franchisor's general counsel.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical, either dental support organisations or auto dealer groups. Cold-email 40 general counsel with a free three-location sample audit. Build scanners on public review data and line up two law firms as referral partners.

title: Signed Eyewitness Network for Ports and Sanctions
angle: Pairing 2: Creator economy & media provenance x Government/public sector/defense/municipal services (signed capture by hobbyist creators x defense/dual-use OSINT)
one_liner: A network of ship, plane and port spotters and local creators paid per provenance-signed capture (verified time, place and device), sold first to maritime insurers and sanctions teams and next to Coast Guard, Navy and intelligence analysts.
customer: Sanctions-compliance teams at banks, commodity traders and marine insurers or P&I brokers ($40-150 per verified task, $2-5K/month watchlist subscriptions). Later buyers are Coast Guard, CBP, NGA and defense OSINT analysts through SBIR or commercial solutions openings.
problem: Open-source analysis is bottlenecked on 'who shot this and when', not on analysis. AI fakes and unverified feeds enter analytic workflows: a SOCOM analyst's chatbot fabricated a cargo manifest and aircraft were airborne before the error was caught, while Maven now has 100K+ users and leaders admit gaps in logistics data visibility. Hobbyist spotters and drone and dashcam creators already sit at chokepoints, but their images cannot be trusted, priced or bought.
solution: Buyers post look-and-verify tasks ('is tanker X at berth Y today?'). Spotters reply with C2PA-signed captures from phones with native content credentials (prior knowledge: recent Pixel and Samsung models). The platform validates the signature chain, GNSS and time, and cross-checks sun angle, weather and AIS, then packages an analyst-ready evidence artifact with a spotter reputation score. Buyers purchase a signed artifact, not labor, so this is not a freelancer marketplace.
why_now: Native camera signing shipped on mainstream phones (prior knowledge) and C2PA reached spec 2.3, so no proprietary hardware is needed. Sanctions and shadow-fleet enforcement and the 2026 Iran conflict raise verification demand, and GenAI.mil put AI summarization in front of 2M users, making trusted ground-truth inputs the scarce resource.
revenue_model: Per-task fees with a 30% platform take, watchlist subscriptions, and government contracts later.
non_obvious_insight: AI is making analysis abundant and cheap while trusted ground truth stays scarce. The hobbyist spotter community is an existing, unpaid, reputation-rich sensor network, and because phones now sign captures a two-person team can build the verification layer instead of hardware.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 spotters from ship- and plane-spotting forums in two port cities. Take 10 paid pilot tasks at about $75 from a marine insurance broker or sanctions consultancy, build the verification pipeline around C2PA validation plus AIS cross-checks, and then apply to an SBIR or commercial solutions opening on commercial ground truth.

title: Compliance-First CDL School Roll-Up for Carriers
one_liner: Buy the clean CDL schools that survived the federal crackdown, run them with AI scheduling and audit-ready records, and get paid per hired graduate by carriers.
customer: Trucking carriers (pay-per-hire or tuition guarantees), students (financed), and workforce boards. School owners are the sellers.
problem: FMCSA removed nearly 3,000 providers from the Training Provider Registry and has thousands more under investigation. The non-domiciled CDL rule effective 16 March 2026 removed an estimated 90,000+ CDLs. Carriers need legitimate, US-domiciled drivers with provable training, and independent schools are mom-and-pop operations with thin documentation, idle trucks and scarce instructors.
solution: Acquire mid-size schools with clean records. AI ops: scheduling that keeps trucks and instructors busy, automatic ELDT and registry records with an audit-ready evidence packet per student, simulators and camera or telematics coaching that shorten range hours, and a placement engine matching graduates to carriers. Carriers pay a bounty per hire and back student financing.
why_now: The 2026 crackdown turned record quality into a scarce, acquirable asset, and capacity is tight. Carriers want vetted sources of drivers, and simulators and telematics are now cheap.
revenue_model: Tuition of $4k to $8k per student (self-pay, financed, or WIOA-funded), carrier placement fees of $3k to $6k per hire, and simulator licensing to smaller schools.
non_obvious_insight: After a regulatory purge, provenance is the product. The school that can prove every training hour becomes a carrier's preferred feeder farm, so audit-ready data is worth more than the trucks. Reputation risk from CDL mills is a barrier to entry for bad actors and a marketing asset for a clean operator.
first_30_days: Sign a letter of intent with one small school owner on seller financing. Sign two regional carriers to a pilot pay-per-hired-graduate agreement. Put cameras and telematics on two training trucks and produce a sample audit packet. Publish pass and placement data.

title: Emerging-Market Multigrade Methods for US Microschools
angle: Education, credentialing and skills after AI x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: License and adapt proven low-cost, paper-based, self-paced multigrade teaching systems from Colombia, Bangladesh and India, and sell them as a turnkey kit and training to US microschools and shrinking rural districts.
customer: Microschool founders and pod networks, including the roughly 1,000 microschools the brief says are in limbo awaiting federal scholarship-credit rules, paying $1,500-5,000 a year. Homeschool co-ops with ESA money and small rural districts forced into combined-grade classes are the next buyers.
problem: One adult with 6-25 kids across several ages is now the standard microschool model. Guides are often uncredentialed (about two-thirds at Alpha School), 48% of microschool students in one dataset have special needs, and most run on screens. 61% of teachers want less device use, and AI tutors have shown no benefit over plain practice in a two-year Tennessee study.
solution: Sequenced, printable learning guides for K-6 math and literacy, peer-tutoring routines, student-run classroom governance, a 2-day guide training plus six weekly remote coaching calls, and paper mastery checkpoints. The checkpoints double as evidence for scholarship-granting organizations and ESA administrators. Licence terms give originators such as Escuela Nueva (Colombia), BRAC's one-room schools (Bangladesh) or Rishi Valley's School in a Box (India) a royalty share, so the deal funds their work too.
why_now: The federal scholarship tax credit starts in 2027 with 31 states opted in and rules still unwritten, so founders are looking for defensible academics. K-12 enrollment is heading from 49.4M to 46.9M by 2031 and more than 1,000 schools closed this year, so multi-age classes are coming to ordinary rural districts. Screen fatigue, AI bans in NYC and LAUSD, and weak AI-tutor evidence all push buyers toward paper and evidence-backed methods.
revenue_model: A one-time kit plus training at $1,500-3,000 per microschool (about $300 per student), a $600-2,400 annual coaching subscription, and district pilots at $15-40k. Royalties of 10-15% go to the licensors.
non_obvious_insight: The US treats one-adult-many-ages classrooms as a Silicon Valley invention. Countries that built them out of necessity decades ago have field-tested materials that are cheap, paper-based, robust to bad connectivity and teacher-light. Those traits match what US buyers suddenly want in 2026: fewer screens, no AI dependence, and documented outcomes. The emerging-market side is the supplier of know-how, not the customer.
first_30_days: Contact the licensors and negotiate a one-subject pilot licence (grades 2-5 math) in English. Print five paper guide sets. Recruit five microschools through founder communities and networks like the National Microschooling Center at $1,200 each. Record baseline scores with NWEA MAP or i-Ready and re-test after 10 weeks so the results become the first case study.

title: Robot Gymnasium Inside a Dead Mall
one_liner: Lease dying mall wings for pennies, stage them as real-world sets, and rent them by the day to robotics startups that need diverse places to collect training data.
customer: Humanoid and manipulation-robotics startups (seed to Series B, 20-200 people) and robot-data vendors. They need varied real environments, teleoperator labor and QA'd data, and they can't build a facility of their own.
problem: Robot foundation models are data-starved. Collecting demonstrations needs varied, realistic settings such as grocery aisles, pharmacies, kitchens, hotel corridors, escalators, elevators and glass doors. Lab space in tech metros is tiny and expensive. At-home gig collection is cheap but noisy and raises privacy issues. Chinese players are building 10,000+ m2 collection campuses, and the US has almost nothing comparable.
solution: Take a short-term license on 30-100k sq ft of a dead mall, often at $0.25-1/sq ft because the owner's alternative is a vacant box. Build 8-10 modular sets from closed-store fixtures and thrift furniture: grocery aisle, pharmacy counter, apartment kitchen and bedroom, laundromat, hotel hallway, office. The mall's escalators, revolving doors, elevators, tile and carpet changes and glass storefronts come free as hard perception cases. Sell each set by the day with a motion-capture and camera rig, calibrated lighting and a teleop station. Add a local, trained teleoperator pool billed per accepted demonstration hour, plus a QA pipeline that delivers clean, labeled data.
why_now: Humanoid and VLA robotics funding is in a data-collection race in 2026. MIT Technology Review has covered gig workers training humanoids at home, and China's state-backed training centers run 100+ robots at a time. Paxini reportedly owns a 12,000 m2 collection facility, and AGIBOT rents robots with operators for about $500/day. Dead-mall owners are more distressed than ever, and cheap rental of a robot plus an operator means small teams need somewhere to use them.
revenue_model: Day-rate per environment ($1.5-4k/day). Per-accepted-hour teleop data fees. Monthly reserved 'bays' for resident robotics teams. Later, a revenue share when customers license the resulting datasets.
non_obvious_insight: For robot learning, messy variety with cheap labor and no neighbors matters more than lab polish. A dead mall is free set design, and its owner will pay to have anchor-store fixtures hauled away. The scarce asset is environment diversity plus ops discipline, and the mall itself is nearly free.
first_30_days: Contact 10 owners of dead or dying malls within driving distance of robotics clusters (Pittsburgh, Boston, Detroit, Austin, exurban Bay Area, Atlanta). Sign one 6-month license and build 3 sets for under $25k. Pre-sell 3 pilot collection weeks to startups through robotics meetups and founder networks, with $10-15k deposits. Hire 4 part-time teleoperators and write the data-QA checklist.

title: Compliance Rail for Verified Bio-AI Labs
one_liner: A 'SOC 2 for AI-directed biology': fast dossiers plus continuous evidence collection that let small labs qualify for, and keep, verified access to frontier bio-AI.
customer: Small biotechs, CROs, academic cores and AI-bio startups applying to verification programs (Anthropic expects hundreds of organizations in week one); later insurers and pharma partners that request attestations.
problem: Trend chain: frontier providers now gate relaxed bio safeguards behind credential, security and ethics-oversight review. Next, each provider and government runs a slightly different program. Then small labs discover they lack security staff, an oversight committee, or records separating AI proposal, human edit and robot execution (a gap Lab Manager flags, since CDC and WHO frameworks predate autonomous systems). Each application becomes bespoke paperwork.
solution: Week 1: a 5-day 'verification-ready' dossier covering security-control mapping (SOC 2 and ISO 27001-lite), personnel credential packet, data-retention and access configuration, and a dual-use risk register. Optionally add a rent-an-oversight-committee: an independent biosafety and dual-use review board with documented minutes. Month 3 onward: connectors to ELN, LIMS, robot logs and AI-provider logs produce an audit trail and a portable attestation that is reused across providers.
why_now: Anthropic's Life Sciences Verification Program launched Sept 17, 2026, with 30-day data retention and 'hundreds of organizations' expected in the first week. Other providers are likely to follow (an inference). Autonomous labs are multiplying with no accountability standard.
revenue_model: $3-8k per dossier, $1.5-4k/month for oversight-committee and evidence subscription, and per-attestation fees from providers or insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Relaxed safeguards become a competitive credential the way SOC 2 became table stakes in SaaS. The bottleneck is not the AI provider's review but small organizations' inability to package proof. Once two or more providers run programs, a portable attestation beats bespoke applications, and the evidence stream also feeds insurers.
first_30_days: Turn the public criteria into a 40-point readiness checklist. Sell a $1.5k readiness review to 20 startups via SynBioBeta and LinkedIn. Partner with an IBC or biosafety consultancy for the oversight-committee product. Ship the dossier template.

title: UL for Talking Toys: Behavioral Safety Lab
one_liner: An independent lab that red-teams AI toys and kid-facing companion gadgets with child personas, then sells scorecards and a 'passed' seal to brands and retailers.
customer: AI-toy brands and ODMs launching in the US, licensors of kids' IP, and big-box and online retailers' product-safety and legal teams, plus toy-industry insurers.
problem: Physical toy labs test lead and choking hazards but nobody tests what a toy says across a 200-turn conversation, whether guardrails drift, where audio goes, or whether privacy claims are true. Late-2025 consumer testing reportedly found AI toys giving inappropriate content (not verified in the brief). Retailers carry the liability, and the FTC's 6(b) inquiry, SB 243 and the amended COPPA rule raise the stakes.
solution: A standard suite of about 300 child-persona conversations (ages 4-12, varied accents), child-style jailbreak probing, sensitive-topic sweeps, long-horizon persona drift, network capture of data flows and retention, and verification of COPPA claims. Deliverables are a scorecard, fix list, re-test and a versioned seal retailers can require.
why_now: Holiday 2026 is the first mass AI-toy season (Mattel-OpenAI partnership, from memory; Character.AI's under-18 exit), and retailers' legal teams need evidence by Q4. The buying window is right now.
revenue_model: $12-40k per product per version, annual retainers for brands, and seal licensing fees.
non_obvious_insight: Retailers, not parents, are the choke point, and they buy assurance rather than products. The test is dynamic (behavior over time) rather than static (materials), which makes it a new category of lab created by regulators' fear.
first_30_days: Buy 10 AI toys and gadgets (about $1.5k) and publish a public holiday AI-toy behavior report with methodology. Send private reports to 5 retailer compliance heads and 10 brands. Offer paid re-tests to any brand that fails.

title: IEEPA Refund Ledger for CPAs and Controllers
one_liner: An accounting workbench that turns IEEPA refund data into correct inventory, cost-of-goods, tax and audit entries.
customer: CPA and advisory firms serving importers, and controllers at $10M-$500M manufacturers and distributors.
problem: About 330,000 importers paid about $166B on 53M entries. CBP had repaid about $86.3B by 2026-07-10, and AD/CVD and liquidated-entry cases come later. Each refund must be split between duty still in inventory, duty already in cost of goods sold, and interest, each with different book and tax treatment (UNICAP, state conformity, LIFO layers). CFOs have no playbook and brokers do not touch accounting.
solution: Import ACE entry-summary exports and broker data. Match each entry line to inventory layers or sales. Compute period-by-period reversal entries. Produce journal entries, a tax memo, a state schedule and a reconciliation to CBP statements. Model cash-tax timing for Q4 estimates. Export to QuickBooks, NetSuite and Sage.
why_now: Refunds are flowing in phases now, with year-end close and Q4 estimated payments (due 2026-12-15 for calendar-year C corporations) approaching.
revenue_model: $750-3k per client engagement through CPA firms. $15-40k a year for white-label licenses. It grows into a standing duty sub-ledger for Section 232 changes.
non_obvious_insight: A refund is an accounting event, not a customs event. Every refund creates an inventory-basis and tax problem the broker will not touch, and the same ledger becomes the duty sub-ledger firms need as Section 232 rates keep changing.
first_30_days: Approach 10 CPA firms with importer clients. Build an Excel and Python prototype on three real entry datasets. Sell the first engagements at about $1.5k. Have a tax partner review the methodology.

title: Guard-Shack Handshake: Stopping Fictitious Pickups at the Gate
one_liner: A free, no-login gate tool for shipper guard shacks that shows the pre-enrolled driver, truck, plate and a one-time PIN, paid for per protected load by brokers and cargo insurers.
customer: Brokers moving high-theft commodities (electronics, copper and other metals, consumer goods, food and beverage) and their cargo and contingent-cargo insurers pay. Shippers get the guard tool free, which is what drives adoption.
problem: CargoNet estimates H1 2026 cargo theft losses above $359M, with Q2 2026 losses of $304.6M (more than double Q2 2025) even though incidents fell, driven by high-value metals and technology. Criminals now compromise legitimate carrier accounts, internet-based phone systems, email and compliance-platform credentials, so the email domain, callback number and vetting badge can all be authentic-looking. Meanwhile at the physical gate a guard checks a load number and a BOL, as in 1995. The load number is a password that the broker has already emailed to dozens of carriers.
solution: At tender, the broker's rate-con flow triggers a driver self-enrollment via SMS link: selfie, CDL photo, truck and trailer plate photos. The system checks how recently the carrier's public contact info changed and whether the enrolling number matches prior loads. The shipper's shipping desk and guard get a web link (no app, no integration) showing the expected driver photo, plate and USDOT number. The driver must speak a PIN issued only through the enrollment. The guard taps match or mismatch and snaps an arrival photo, and any mismatch alerts the broker and shipper instantly. The receiver gets the same flow at delivery. Aggregated data goes to insurers.
why_now: The 2026 CargoNet reports describe impersonation-based theft as systematic and scalable, with credential and phone-system compromise defeating digital-only checks. Montgomery (May 2026) raised broker liability, and insurers are now asking brokers for controls. The Jan 2026 FMCSA rule means a broker who pays a big theft claim can drop below the bond threshold and face suspension.
revenue_model: $2-$5 per protected load charged to brokers, plus an insurer revenue share or bounty for verified low-loss books. Later, sell a 'verified pickup' certificate to cargo insurers in exchange for lower deductibles.
non_obvious_insight: The thief needs two things, a load number and a plausible carrier identity, and the broker hands out both freely. Nobody has redesigned the 30-second guard-shack transaction because shippers feel the cargo is no longer theirs once the BOL is signed, so the party that eats the loss (broker or insurer) has to fund a free tool for the party that controls the gate. The best fraud tell is not the carrier's score but the age of its contact info: hijacked carriers show new phones and emails days before booking. Brokers whisper this in fraud groups but no product sells it.
first_30_days: Sign 3 brokers hauling metals or electronics and pick 5 recurring shipper docks. Build a web-only MVP (SMS enrollment plus guard view) and run the PINs manually. Pilot 100 loads, measuring driver friction (target under 90 seconds) and catch rate with seeded red-team tests. Get one cargo insurer or MGA to review the pilot data for a premium credit.

title: Employer-Backed Block Leases for Hourly Workers
one_liner: A broker that packages 20-100 unit block leases in concession-heavy buildings, backed by an employer's credit guarantee and payroll deduction, to cut rent for hourly workers without raising wages.
customer: Hospital systems, school districts, hotels, casinos and retailers with recruiting and turnover pain, paired with owners of lease-up and high-concession properties who pay the placement fee.
problem: A typical retail worker earns $34,436 against $71,172 needed for a typical $1,779 apartment. Employers lose workers to housing costs, while owners in lease-up hand out 15-37% concessions to anonymous renters and carry 34 days of vacancy.
solution: Negotiate discounted block rents in exchange for guaranteed occupancy. The employer provides a credit guarantee rather than a subsidy, plus optional payroll deduction, and we run eligibility, lease templates, guarantee underwriting and monitoring. The tenant's discount is funded by the owner's savings on concessions, marketing, vacancy and turnover.
why_now: The rental glut and record concessions give owners a reason to trade price for certainty. Employer labor tightness is high, and traditional locators ignore blocks because commissions are small.
revenue_model: Owner-paid placement fee of 3-4% of first-year rent, employer platform fee of $8-15 per enrolled unit per month, and an optional guarantee premium.
non_obvious_insight: The landlord is buying occupancy certainty, not tenants, and avoided concession, vacancy and turnover can approach 10-15% of annual rent, more than a free month per tenant. Employers can create affordability by lending credit instead of paying wages, which also helps them avoid taxable-benefit complications.
first_30_days: Pick Austin or Atlanta. Get three owners with 300+ unit lease-ups to sign a 10%-off block-lease term sheet. Pitch five HR or recruiting heads at hospital and community-college systems. Run one 25-unit pilot and collect the placement fee.

title: Immigration Deadline Sentinel for Work-Permit Households
one_liner: The wealthy keep immigration counsel on retainer to calendar, file early and bridge gaps; for $20/mo, give H-4, OPT, asylum-applicant and DACA households an encrypted deadline vault and family-readiness plan.
customer: Households whose work authorization depends on renewable USCIS documents: H-4/L-2 spouses with EADs, F-1 OPT/STEM OPT students, asylum applicants, DACA recipients, and pending adjustment applicants. Sold at $20/mo per household, or $4-8 per head through employers, university international offices, credit unions and churches.
problem: DHS ended automatic 540-day EAD extensions for renewals filed on or after 30 October 2025. USCIS advises filing up to 180 days early, yet some I-765 categories are reported at many months to a year or more, so gaps in work authorization mean lost jobs, licenses and health coverage. Rich families' lawyers prevent this by tracking every date; ordinary families rely on memory and WhatsApp.
solution: An end-to-end-encrypted vault, on-device where possible: photograph an EAD, I-94 or I-797 and it extracts dates and builds a household calendar (EAD file window opening at day 180, AR-11 address change within 10 days, OPT unemployment day counter, I-751, N-400 windows, passport expiries). It pre-fills renewal packets for attorney review, generates employer bridging letters, and monitors case status. For cases outside normal processing times it prepares a congressional-inquiry package. It adds a family-readiness plan (power of attorney, standby guardianship for children, contact tree, know-your-rights card). Flat-fee referrals go to attorneys and DOJ-accredited representatives. It is software and documents, not legal advice.
why_now: The October 2025 interim final rule ended automatic extensions, processing times are long, USCIS moved to a new I-765 form version (mandatory from March 2026), and enforcement anxiety is high in 2026. Employers and universities are scrambling to protect workers.
revenue_model: $20/mo per household; $3-6 per employee per month for employer or university dashboards; flat referral fees from partner attorneys; enterprise HR reporting tier.
non_obvious_insight: Wealthy people's immigration counsel adds most of its value before a crisis, by calendaring, filing early and pre-drafting backups, which software can supply for a fraction of the cost. Privacy-by-design (end-to-end encryption so a subpoena or breach yields nothing) is not just compliance but the differentiator for a population that fears data exposure. The paying wedge is the professional H-4/OPT segment and their employers, not the most vulnerable households.
first_30_days: Build a WhatsApp and spreadsheet MVP that ingests document photos and sends reminders. Partner with 2 immigration attorneys on flat-fee referral, 3 university international offices, and H-4 spouse and OPT Facebook groups. Enroll 100 households free, convert to $20/mo, and pilot with one employer HR team.

title: Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: Catch dealers that sell floored cars and pocket the payoff by watching the one signal an F&I insider knows can't be hidden: the VIN disappears from public listings but the floorplan payoff never arrives.
customer: Floorplan lenders and their auditors: independent floorplan companies, captive finance arms, regional banks and credit unions with dealer lines, and warehouse lenders that fund subprime and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Pay $15 to $30 per monitored dealer per month plus enterprise data fees.
problem: A dealer sells out of trust when it sells a floored car and does not pay the lender's payoff on time. It is how small cash squeezes become fraud. Ford and Stellantis are in court against Sky Auto Mall over exactly this, and floorplan use is heavier with inventory at roughly 88 days' supply and rates at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps. Lenders police it with periodic on-site audits (monthly, quarterly or random), so a dealer can sell for weeks before anyone looks. The dealer's own delay makes it worse, since contracts in transit stretch to a week or more before the lender funds, so honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books.
solution: Daily VIN-level monitoring of each lender's floored inventory against public and licensed listing feeds from the dealer's site and the major marketplaces. When a floored VIN disappears from listings, the tool starts a clock. It cross-checks against lender-provided payoff events and, where available, title and registration transactions and electronic lien releases. If no payoff shows within the expected window (about 7 to 10 days for a clean deal, longer for slow lenders), it flags the dealer and VIN and ranks risk by dealer history and how many VINs are in the queue. Flags trigger a spot audit or a curtailment call. A dealer-facing version shows honest dealers exactly which VINs look 'unpaid' so they can fix processing before the lender calls, and it doubles as an early-warning feed for warehouse lenders.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put double-pledged collateral and verification failures in front of every subprime lender and their investors. In March 2026 Ford and Stellantis were still litigating floorplan fraud against Sky Auto Mall. Rising inventory and higher rates increase floorplan reliance. Public listing feeds and cheap LLM data extraction make VIN-level monitoring practical for a team of three.
revenue_model: Per-dealer monthly monitoring fee, a per-alert fee on confirmed cases, and enterprise data licensing to captives and ABS or warehouse investors. Upsell: a contracts-in-transit tracker that gives dealers a lender-verified funding timeline and later powers same-day advances against verified contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The only place SOT cannot hide is the retail listing. A dealer will lie about payoffs, backdate titles and pay one lender with another's money, but it still has to take a car off its website when it sells it, because customers and marketplaces punish stale listings. Auditors check what is on the lot; nobody checks what left the internet. An F&I person knows this from watching sold cars vanish from the site the same day the deal is signed, and from knowing how long a funded payoff should really take.
first_30_days: Build a scraper for a pilot set of 50 dealer inventory pages and a listing-history log. Backtest on cases visible in public court filings (the Sky Auto Mall filings and a handful of others) to show the signal would have fired weeks earlier. Approach three small independent floorplan lenders and two credit unions with dealer floorplan lines, offer a free 60-day pilot on their books, and charge $20 per dealer per month after proving at least one real catch.

title: SOC 2 for Rent-Pricing Algorithms
one_liner: An independent audit and continuous-monitoring attestation proving an operator's revenue-management tool uses lawful inputs and real human decisions.
customer: Multifamily operators (5,000-100,000 units) using RealPage, Yardi or Entrata-style pricing in ban or enforcement jurisdictions, defendants under consent decrees needing monitors, and their insurers and lenders.
problem: Pricing tools are now legal liabilities: New York State (Dec 2025) and Berkeley ban them, San Diego levies $1,000 per violation and a UDR class action was filed, private settlements exceed $500M, and Pinnacle signed a decree Sept 4 with Camden the lone unsettled original defendant. Vendors named in suits cannot credibly certify themselves, and operators cannot prove where prices come from.
solution: Audit data lineage (any nonpublic competitor inputs, data age), analyze auto-accept and override rates and human-decision documentation, map jurisdictional exposure, and issue a signed attestation with quarterly evidence reports. License the tooling to monitors of consent decrees.
why_now: Decrees can require compliance officers and monitors, city bans are multiplying, and insurers and lenders are beginning to ask for proof.
revenue_model: $20-60K annual attestation per operator, monitor tool licenses, and insurer or broker referral arrangements.
non_obvious_insight: Independence is the product, and vendors in litigation cannot sell it. As with SOC 2 in cloud, the standard will belong to whoever writes v1 and gets insurers and lenders to accept it. Acceptance rates are the observable that plaintiffs and monitors will use.
first_30_days: Draft a 'Rent Pricing Compliance Standard v0.1' with antitrust counsel. Offer a free exposure scan to 30 operators and sign three paid design partners at a $10K discount. Approach two monitor firms and a D&O broker.
